articles.title: Three countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and Italy
articles.summary: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay. ‘Achtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did…
body: Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.

My husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the old Gasthof Alte Post, we’d bought a loaf from the bäckerei, climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.

We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispy bitterballen before boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.

articles.title: A new start after 60: I’m 92 and cycling is my life – despite the crash that left me unconscious
articles.summary: Arthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every year. When Arthur Plummer retired at 65, he bought a secondhand bicycle.
body: “I love cycling,” he says. “Wherever I go, even if I ride on the same roads, there’s something new happening. When I get on my bike, I feel great. I come home at about 3pm and I feel exhausted. However, it’s the nicest feeling. It’s exhilarating, and it’s resulted in me being extremely healthy.”

Even when, in his late 80s, Plummer developed polymyalgia rheumatica (an inflammatory condition that causes pain, stiffness and inflammation in the shoulders, neck and hips) and was unable to walk, cycling helped him to move again. “I was in a wheelchair and I would sit outside in my driveway and people would go by and I felt trapped,” he says. “I can’t walk,” he thought, “but if I can get on my bike, I bet I could ride.” So that’s what he did.

Although his legs are strong, walking is still uncomfortable; he has a shortened stride and sometimes struggles to keep up with his wife and friends on holiday. Cycling, on the other hand, brings freedom. Plummer has cycled “on every street you can go on” within 100 sq miles (260 sq km) of where he lives. He often takes his bike on the bus so that he can explore farther afield. “I’m looking for new vistas,” he says.

articles.title: The agony of life with chronic body odour: ‘I swear I’ve tried every deodorant’
articles.summary: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers. If Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window.
body: She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.”

For more than a decade, 66-year-old Hayat lived with bromhidrosis: chronic body odour. Though the term applies to BO from any cause, including poor hygiene, it is more typically driven by a bacterial imbalance or other health issue.

For those individuals, it’s not a question of bathing more often, or switching to a higher-strength deodorant: their body is working against them, and the impact can be ruinous. “Fifteen minutes after a shower, they’ve already started smelling,” says Chris Callewaert, a senior research fellow at Ghent University, Belgium, and one of the few scientists in the world specialising in body odour.

Callewaert describes bromhidrosis as a natural bodily process gone awry, most typically involving the apocrine glands. These are concentrated around the armpits, breasts and groin, and secrete lipids, steroids and proteins. This sweat itself is odourless; BO is produced by the natural bacteria on the skin and inside the hair follicles as they digest the fatty secretion.
points: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers.

articles.title: Tattie scones and scrambled eggs, toasted bannocks with honey butter and roast plums – Anna Higham’s big breakfast recipes
articles.summary: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter. I’ve long wanted a space to cook the food that really excites me, and Clementine, which opens its doors in north London next month, is…
body: First, make the morning rolls. Combine the dry ingredients in a bowl, then rub in the lard. Add the water, mix to form a rough dough, then cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes.

Knead the dough until it feels smooth, springy and has good stretch – about 10 minutes in a mixer on medium speed, 25 minutes by hand. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container, cover with a damp tea towel and leave for about an hour to double in size.

Turn out the dough on to a well-floured surface, roll it into a rectangle, then divide into 12 equal pieces of about 120g each. Pinch the four corners of one piece of dough into the centre, then flip over. Allow the dough to stick slightly to the worktop and, with a cupped hand, work it into a tight ball. Now use a dough scraper to release it from the bench, then transfer to a lined, high-sided baking tray. Repeat with the remaining pieces of dough, spacing them evenly apart. Sprinkle each with a little flour, cover with a damp cloth and refrigerate overnight.
Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, then bake the rolls for 25-30 minutes, until dark and “well fired” on top; remove and leave to cool slightly.

articles.title: For Joshua Ewusie, Faux Flowers and Leather Lace Explore the Politics of Taste
articles.summary: The spring 2027 collection of NEWGEN designer Ewusie turned to the domestic codes of migrant homes to push his signature leatherwork somewhere softer.
body: Joshua Ewusie’s spring 2027 collection began at home: in the front rooms of migrant households, where faux flowers sat atop plastic tablecloths and colorful crochet throws.

“The home is the first place where you start to get an idea of creating an aesthetic, where you realize things have been put somewhere intentionally,” said the London designer, now on his third collection as a British Fashion Council NEWGEN recipient. His own memories returned him to his grandmother’s and Ghanaian family’s homes, whose front rooms were salons and meeting places. “I thought a lot about women in our cultures who see the home as an opportunity to show everything that is precious to them,” he said.

For the collection, titled In Lieu of Flowers, Ewusie also looked to Michael McMillan’s The Front Room, a study of the domestic interiors of post-war Caribbean migrants in Britain, and began reconsidering the objects sometimes consigned to the category of kitsch or “cheap.” Why, he wondered, should the pattern of a plastic tablecloth be deemed bad taste when its origins lie in handmade lace? The question proved fertile ground for a designer already known for making leather do unexpected and gorgeous things.
points: The spring 2027 collection of NEWGEN designer Ewusie turned to the domestic codes of migrant homes to push his signature leatherwork somewhere softer.

articles.title: Vogue World Milano: What Does Made in Italy Stand for Today?
articles.summary: Over the past two years, Made in Italy has been rocked by allegations of worker exploitation, an impending talent shortage and rising costs. But the history of craftsmanship and quality remains.
body: “In Italy, we compare everything to food,” says Alberto Candiani, the fourth-generation owner of leading Italian denim producer Candiani Denim. “We claim it is the best food in the world — and it might be — but what makes it special is the way we cook it. We take our time, we use the right ingredients. It’s very regional. All over Italy, you will find different nuances and details. Our approach to fashion is the same.”

Everywhere you go in Italy, from Piedmont to Prato, fashion brands and suppliers share some version of this sentiment. They say ‘Made in Italy’ is more than a label; it’s a source of regional and national pride — a blend of art and engineering, cultivated by centuries of craftsmanship, passed down from generation to generation. “It’s a way of life,” says Luca Sburlati, CEO of Pattern Group and president of trade organization Confindustria Moda. “And it’s the last complete fashion supply chain in Europe, where you have everything from the raw material to the finished product in one country.”
Italian supply chains are at risk of losing their know-how. Suppliers and brands alike are pinning their hopes on new educational programmes.

articles.title: Made in Italy: Meet the Makers
articles.summary: Behind every Made in Italy product are artisans who have spent decades honing their craft. But artisanship isn’t limited to skills like embroidery or leatherwork; it’s in every step of the supply chain.
body: On Tuesday, Vogue World: Milano will take over Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II to celebrate Italian craftsmanship on the world stage. It’s a profound moment to reflect on Made in Italy and reinforce fashion’s commitment to craft. In the age of AI and mass manufacturing, products that are forged by hand, honoring artisanal crafts passed down through generations, are a differentiator. Unsurprisingly, craft is quickly becoming luxury’s most valuable currency.

My task as pattern-maker is to receive a photo or drawing — and sometimes specific measurements — and create a digital pattern that is consistent with the expectations of the brand. It has to be industrializable and reproducible, and I need to reach the final version with as few prototypes as possible. It requires sensitivity, culture and a knowledge of materials, workmanship and product.

articles.title: How to Spend a Day Experiencing the Real Milan
articles.summary: A brief guide to some of Milan’s most timeless hidden gems, ahead of Vogue World 2026: Milano.
body: “Yes, my friend, Milan is truly beautiful, and believe me when I say that it sometimes takes real determination to resist its temptations and stay focused on work,” wrote the acclaimed Italian novelist Giovanni Verga in a letter to fellow writer Luigi Capuana in 1873. Born in Vizzini, a small town in the province of Catania, Verga was won over by Milan soon after he moved to the city, finding it a rich source of creative inspiration.

When Verga wrote his letter, he was a new arrival in Milan with all the enthusiasm of a recent convert, but his sentiments are also shared by those born and raised in the city. Many locals are almost obsessively determined to preserve their favorite rituals and support their most beloved insider spots, grounded in tradition and the authentic spirit of Milan. While there will always be exciting new openings, it is often the old favorites—places that have been visited many times over the years and decades—that provide the setting for the most lasting memories.
